sections.html:
The Winnebago County Register of Deeds is where Oshkosh-area property records live, along with vital records and military discharges. The land side of the office files deeds, land contracts, mortgages, UCC realty filings, plats, certified survey maps and federal tax liens.

When a house in the county sells, the seller's deed to the buyer is filed here, and staff take the state transfer fee at that same visit. The phone number is 920-232-3390.

Filing a deed costs $30 flat, and page count does not change it. The county's fee schedule traces that to Wisconsin Act 314 of 2010, and Wis. Stat. 59.43(2)(ag) sets the identical $30 for any recordable document.

ServiceWinnebago County charge
Filing a deed, mortgage, land contract or satisfaction$30, flat
Plain copy of a filed document$2 for page one, then $1 per added page
Certification of a copy$1 extra
Subdivision, cemetery or condominium plat$50
State transfer fee$3 per $1,000 of value, rounded up to the next hundred, unless exempt

The office takes cash, money orders and personal checks. A card works only for orders placed in the office, and amounts up to $50 draw a $2.50 surcharge. Whoever asks for a service pays in advance, so have payment ready before the deed goes in.

Thirty cents per $100 of value is the transfer fee, and the seller owes it. Staff collect it as the deed is handed in. The grantor, meaning the seller, bears the fee under state law, and any piece of $100 is charged as a whole $100.

The whole price counts. Wis. Stat. 77.21(3) measures a sale by every dollar paid or promised, including the balance of any lien on the property. For a gift, or a deed with token consideration, value means the likely open-market price. For a land contract, it means the total principal the buyer agrees to pay.

Of each fee collected, the county retains 20 percent by statute and sends the remainder to the state. The register is not obliged to test the reported value or an exemption claim, which leaves the buyer and seller answerable for their own figures.

A transfer escapes the fee only if it fits a category in Wis. Stat. 77.25, and the deed must give the reason by subsection number. These matter most to families and to sellers under pressure:

  • Gifts or near-gifts within a family: parent to child, stepparent to stepchild, parent to a son-in-law or daughter-in-law, or grandparent to grandchild.
  • A transfer between a person and a domestic partner.
  • Property that passes by will, by descent or by survivorship.
  • Foreclosure and deed-in-lieu transfers to a mortgage holder or a land contract seller.
  • A sale made for delinquent taxes or assessments.
  • A conveyance of real estate valued at $1,000 or less.

Exemptions are read narrowly. Court decisions summarized alongside the statute show that a move between two entities can be taxed even when family members own both. If a deed involves an LLC or a trust, check the exemption wording or ask the Register of Deeds before signing.

You file a Real Estate Transfer Return with the Wisconsin Department of Revenue, then bring the receipt or exemption number along with the deed. Seller and buyer both sign. Without a finished return and the fee, the register has no authority to take the conveyance.

Filing now happens in My Tax Account, where nobody has to register or make a username and password. In that system you can submit, review or amend a return. The department's RETR page offers user guides, a walk-through video and a list of transfer fee exemptions. Send questions to retr@wisconsin.gov.

Every conveyance recorded here needs either an electronic transfer receipt plus the fee or an exemption number. Wis. Stat. 77.255 excuses a few exempt transfers from any return, so if you cannot tell which kind of deed you have, ask the register's office.

Deeds that miss the state format may be turned away. Wis. Stat. 59.43(2m) sets the rules, among them:

  • A plain title for the document, set 0.5 inch to 6 inches below the top edge of page one.
  • An empty block of at least 3 inches by 3 inches in the upper right of page one, inside the margins, reserved for the recording stamp area.
  • Return-to information on page one, unless the document is recorded electronically.
  • The parcel identification number of every parcel involved, where the county requires it.
  • Pages 8.5 inches wide and 11 or 14 inches long, not hinged or joined along the top or sides.

The largest sheet allowed is 8.5 by 14 inches, one side of a sheet counts as a page, and an attached rider is a page of its own. Title companies and attorneys normally handle formatting in a sale. A seller drafting a quitclaim or family deed alone should check each item before mailing.

Since May 1, 2023, paper documents are recorded with no stamp, and the recorded version comes back to you by electronic means. Submit a signed SWIFT Agreement with your document to reach the official copy. You get a link that works for 7 days and prints up to 3 copies; after 3 copies or 7 days you pay regular copy fees.

Thirty days after recording, the paper original is shredded. To save it, include a self-addressed envelope with enough postage, or pick it up at the office within those 30 days, beginning the second business day after recording. It has no stamp and is not the official document. A list of companies that e-record real estate documents for Winnebago County is also available from the county.

Public terminals inside the office let you search, and paid online programs reach the same records. Records mostly reach back to 1850, and indexes to 1935. The office prefers appointments, offered in morning blocks (8:30 to 11:00 a.m.) and afternoon blocks (1:30 to 3:30 p.m.). Walk-ins are welcome on a first come basis, behind anyone who booked.

Tapestry serves occasional online users in real estate work. Laredo suits title firms and anyone who needs daily access. Both carry support and maintenance fees. Want to look at a recorded mortgage, an earlier deed or a lien before you list? Start at the terminals.

sections.h2: Check the county before you record
sections.html:
Oshkosh anchors the Oshkosh-Neenah metropolitan area, which is this county, home to 171,730 people in 2020. Oshkosh, Neenah, Omro, Menasha and Appleton are its cities, but Appleton lies mostly in Outagamie and Calumet counties and Menasha partly in Calumet County. An Appleton or Menasha mailing address can therefore sit in a different county than you assume.

Settle which county applies at the start, because the deed is recorded where the land lies.

faqs.q: What does recording a Winnebago County deed cost?
faqs.a: $30 for each document, whatever its length. Copies cost $2 for page one and $1 for every page after, with $1 more if you want it certified.

faqs.q: Who is responsible for the state transfer fee?
faqs.a: The seller does, in the role of grantor. At 30 cents per $100 of value, which the county words as $3 per $1,000 rounded up to the next hundred, the fee is collected as the deed is handed over.

faqs.q: Is a transfer return required before recording?
faqs.a: Nearly always. Recording requires a return signed by both parties, along with the fee or an exemption number. File it in My Tax Account, where no registration is needed.

faqs.q: Can I get an official copy of my deed after recording?
faqs.a: Yes. Submit a signed SWIFT Agreement with the document and the office sends a 7-day link for printing up to 3 copies. Later copies cost the standard fee.

faqs.q: How do I reach the Winnebago County Register of Deeds?
faqs.a: Phone 920-232-3390. Records on file include deeds, mortgages, land contracts, plats and vital records, and the public terminals are open by appointment or on a walk-in basis.
